messages.subject: [S] Information on S-News
messages.body_plain:
INFORMATION ON S-NEWS

Please save this information for future reference, especially to
modify your subscription or unsubscribe in the future.

The full introduction message contains additional information on the
following topics.  

1. S-news objectives and appropriate use.
2. S-news addresses and subscriptions.
3. To unsubscribe...
4. Replying to messages on S-news.
5. General guidelines for posting to S-news. 
6. S-news archives.
7. Mail exploders. 
8. Who maintains the s-news list?
9. What should I do if I have questions or comments about list policies or 
        management?  (The "s-news-advisory" list.)
10. Features of the Washington University list server.
11. Important list management commands.

To obtain the full message, send a message to 

        s-news-request at wubios.wustl.edu

containing the single line in the BODY of the message:

        intro s-news

or point your Web browser at:

        http://www.biostat.wustl.edu/s-news/s-news-intro.html
-----------------------------------------------------------

TO UNSUBSCRIBE

Use one of the following forms, sent in the BODY of a
message to 
        s-news-request at wubios.wustl.edu
referring to the appropriate list (regular delivery or daily digest),
and including the address you are subscribed under only if it is different
from your current mailing address.

                unsubscribe s-news
                unsubscribe s-news myname at my.address
                unsubscribe s-news-digest
                unsubscribe s-news-digest myname at my.address
-----------------------------------------------------------

S-NEWS OBJECTIVES AND APPROPRIATE USE

S-news is the discussion group on the S and S-plus systems for
statistics, graphics, and programming.  Appropriate topics must be
related to S/S-plus, including programming and usage questions and
suggestions, problem reports, and announcements of new software
(contributed and commercial), books and articles, and conferences and
educational events.  Short job announcements are also acceptable.  Long
advertisements and commercial messages that are not specifically relevant
to S/S-plus are not acceptable.
-----------------------------------------------------------

S-NEWS ADDRESSES

Mail for posting to the S-news list should be sent to:

     s-news at wubios.wustl.edu

All subscription and unsubscription requests and other list management 
commands should be sent to

     s-news-request at wubios.wustl.edu

Messages that require human intervention should be sent to

     s-news-owner at wubios.wustl.edu

but you should make use of the automatic list processor commands whenever
they cover the situation.
-----------------------------------------------------------

IMPORTANT LIST MANAGEMENT COMMANDS

All Majordomo list management commands should be sent to
s-news-request at wubios.wustl.edu.  The command (or multiple commands)
should be in the body of the message, not in the subject line.  If your
mailer puts a signature at the end of the message, put the command
        end 
after your list commands so the signature is not interpreted as
commands.  NEVER send commands to s-news!  (NEVER!)

A full list of Majordomo commands can be obtained by sending the command
        help

To subscribe to the list, send the command
        subscribe s-news
or for the digest version, 
        subscribe s-news-digest
You will be sent a confirmation message to which you must reply to make
sure that you actually desired to subscribe.  This is intended to prevent
forged subscriptions.  Note that subscriptions to the immediate-delivery
and digest versions are handled like two separate lists, so if you want to
switch from immediate delivery to digest, you must unsubscribe to s-news
and subscribe to s-news-digest.

If you want to subscribe using a different address than the one you are
sending from, use the command
        subscribe s-news myname at my.address

To unsubscribe, send one of the following commands as appropriate:
        unsubscribe s-news
        unsubscribe s-news-digest
        unsubscribe s-news myname at my.address
        unsubscribe s-news-digest myname at my.address

>Does anyone know a C++ compiler that works well with Blitz++ and S-Plus
>under Linux on an Intel based computer?  Conversely, does anyone have
>experience with a C++ compiler that I ought definitely to avoid?

The KAI is the compiler usually quoted as working with Blitz. I think
they have a Linux version. I don't know how it interacts with C++. I think
you'll have problems, but I don't know.

Do you really want to use Blitz? Do you really need that last bit of speed?
I would recommend my matrix library in preference if it has the facilities you
need. I think Blitz is far to close to the "bleeding edge" to be recommended
for general use. I have never tried to interface my package to Splus so
I can't help you there. See my web page at webnz.com/robert for details of my
matrix library and also for references to other people's libraries.

Robert

messages.subject: [S] multicomp issues
messages.body_plain:
I have had some difficulties with the multicomp() function from Splus 4.5
for Windows in its multicomp.default form, when the mean (estimates) vector
(x),
covariance matrix (vmat), and linear combination matrix (lmat)
are given explicitly.   An edited multicomp.default() function
is in the attached file mymcdef.ssc .   The original multicomp.default()
uses the S object k for the number of estimates: x: k, vmat: kxk .
The modified function introduces kk for the number of linear combinations,
so that lmat is k x kk.   This implies editing the default lmat,
and, when comparisons = "mca" or "mcc", generating labels from the column
names of lmat instead of from the names of x.

Also attached is an edited plot method for multicomp, which allows the user
to choose the number of comparisons on each graph, file myplotm.txt

Colin Goodall
Risk Adjustment Inc.

messages.subject: Comment on: [S] quick question about apply
messages.subject_clean: Comment on: [S] quick question about apply
messages.body_plain:
It is perhaps worth noting that the approach below is somewhat inefficient
in that:
(1) Each row must be ordered
(2) Looping (via apply) is explicitly used.
(3) The overhead of S-Plus function calls is incurred

A more efficient way to do it would be to use pmax and subscripting, a la:

rep(1:4,each=length(v1))[pmax(v1,v2,v3,v4)==c(v1,v2,v3,v4)]

Although I doubt this would make much practical difference for 4 vectors of
length even a few thousand, avoiding sorting (order n log(n)) when maxing
will do (order n), and avoiding loops and function calls in S-Plus when
subscripting can be (easily) used are generally worthwhile habits I believe.

Comments and nicer solutions welcome!

Bert Gunter
Biometrics Research RY 70-38
Merck & Company
P.O. Box 2000
Rahway, NJ 07065-0900
Phone: (732) 594-7765   Fax: (732) 594-1565

messages.subject: Corrections ( I hope) to Comment on: [S] quick question about ap ply
messages.subject_clean: Corrections ( I hope) to Comment on: [S] quick question about ap ply
messages.body_plain:
Doug Bates politely pointed out that I got my previous post  all fouled up.

My original "avoid the apply" one-liner misorders things and should be
changed to:

x1_rep(1:4,length(v1))[t(matrix(pmax(v1,v2,v3,v4)==c(v1,v2,v3,v4),ncol=4))]

Unfortunately, this still bombs if maxes occur more than once in a row. It
must be modified with:

lgc<-matrix(pmax(v1,v2,v3,v4)==c(v1,v2,v3,v4),ncol=4)
z<-lgc[,1]
for (i in 2:4){
    lgc[,i]<-(lgc[,i]>z)  #This eliminates the extra maxes
    z[lgc[,i]] <-T
}
rep(1:4, length(z))[t(lgc)]

I admit that this is no longer a quick one-liner and that it uses a loop --
but of length 3 rather than the length of the vectors.  Of course,  it still
avoids the quite considerable costs of apply and completely ordering the
rows.

Of course, one could do it more simply by imitating pmax directly:

z_cbind(v1,v2,v3,v4)
best <- rep(1,length(v1))
r<-v1
for (i in 2:4) {
        y <- z[,i]>r
        r[y] <- z[y,i]
        best[y] <- i
      }
best

This again violates the "one-liner" request of the original post, but the
solution is quite simple I think.
For the heck of it, I compared timings on my (pentium, 266 mhz, NT4, S4.5)
PC for the two approaches with 4 vectors of length 9000. The apply()
one-liner took 15 seconds and the little program above took 1.1. This seems
to me to be a not inconsiderable loss of efficiency, although, waiting 14
seconds more is a mere piffle for a one-time only task.

My thanks to Doug and apologies to all for bad programming.However, I hope
the point I wanted to make -- avoiding apply() in favor of simple
subscripting can make a large difference in efficiency -- is still clear.

Bert Gunter

messages.body_plain:
On Mon, 4 Jan 1999, Gunter, Bert wrote:

> For the heck of it, I compared timings on my (pentium, 266 mhz, NT4, S4.5)
> PC for the two approaches with 4 vectors of length 9000. The apply()
> one-liner took 15 seconds and the little program above took 1.1. This seems
> to me to be a not inconsiderable loss of efficiency, although, waiting 14
> seconds more is a mere piffle for a one-time only task.

As a coda to that, in S-PLUS 5.0r3 the one-liner takes 9 minutes and the
program 0.18 secs. You do notice the difference!  There are tremendous
differences in efficiency between versions of S-PLUS, and it seems you do
really want to avoid apply and friends in 5.0. (For reference, the times
unde S-PLUS 3.4 are 14 seconds and 0.14 secs: Sun Ultra 1/170 running
Solaris 2.6.) 

If you really want to do this efficiently, nothing beats compiled code
(especially if you want to handle ties consistently).  My library nnet has
a function max.col to find the columns of a matrix with the largest
entries in each row, breaking ties at random. That _is_ fast enough for
all practical purposes (0.05 secs in this example). (For some pattern
recognition applications I need to predict posterior probabilities and
find the largest at several thousand points, repeatedly.) 

--

messages.subject: Re: [S] for() and process variance
messages.body_plain:
Renaud Lancelot asks:
> 
> I posted this message some days ago but it probably vanished
> between champagne bubles...

I don't think so.  I think it may have simply been that your
solution was not all that bad...

> I would like to compute the process variance as defined in
> Diggle, Liang & Zeger (1994), Analysis of longitudinal data,
> p.51:
> 
> sigma^2 = mean( .5 * (y_ij - y_mk)^2 ),
> with i, m indices for subjects (i != m),
>      j, k indices for time
> 
> I wrote the following small function, but could not find a way
> to avoid the for() loop:
> 
> process.variance <- function(subj, resp) {
>   lst <- unique(subj)
>   sq  <- 0
>   n   <- 0
>   for(i in 1:length(lst)){
>     cond <- subj==lst[i]
>     v <- as.vector(outer(resp[cond], resp[!cond],
>                          function(x,y)
>                             0.5*(x-y)^2))             
>     sq <- sq + sum(v)
>     n  <- n  + length(v)
>   }
>   sq / n
> }
> 
> Would someone teach me how to do it better ?  I am working with
> S+ 4.5r3 for Win95.

I'm going to stick my neck out here and again say I don't think
this is such a bad way of doing it.  In fact it might be the best
way in straight S code.  When you think about it what you want to
do is take the matrix

M <- outer(resp, resp, function(x, y) (x-y)^2)/2

and average the entries, but omitting those corresponding to
differences within individuals.  (If the individuals are adjacent
these will be in a series of irregularly sized diagonal blocks.)

OK, here's a way of doing it that suppresses all mention of for()
loops:

process.var2 <- function(resp, subj) {
        M <- outer(resp, resp, function(x, y) (x-y)^2)/2
        mask <- outer(subj, subj, "!=")
        sum(mask*M)/sum(mask)
}

But the problem is you need to hold two *huge* matrices in memory
rather than a succession of much smaller ones.  I think I'd go
for the loop solution, but you might try some resource monitorings.

In my view it is a mistake to think that a for- loop solution is
_necessarily_ the worst way of doing something.

> Many thanks in advance and happy new year from Senegal !

and likewise from a blazingly hot Adelaide, where today it is 40C.

Bill Venables.

messages.subject: [S] Re: Ripley's Coda and apply()
messages.body_plain:
Last comment (I promise!)

Bill Dunlap of Mathsoft sent me what I think is a very clever (but tricky?)
solution to determining the columns in which the maxes occur in the rows of
a matrix. Here 'tis:

f4 <- function(mat) {
        col.mat <- rep(1:ncol(mat), rep(nrow(mat), ncol(mat))) # col(mat)
        row.mat <- rep(1:nrow(mat), ncol(mat)) # row(mat)
        col.mat[order(row.mat, mat)][(1:nrow(mat)) * ncol(mat)]
}

I like this best of all. It uses compiled code through order()  to avoid
apply()'s function call overhead and any explicit looping. The additional
cost of complete sorting has little practical impact.

However, I find Ripley's coda comments troubling. So despite what I said
earlier, may I raise the following questions:  Given that (a)subscripting
solutions require cleverness; i.e., for most users apply() is simpler and
more natural; and (b) Ripley's coda shows that really shocking penalties can
be incurred in 5.0 for using apply(); => were the right design decisions
made for 5.0? It seems to me that programmability considerations may be
taking precedence over usability -- certainly not a boon from a marketing
standpoint, anyway . I know this is an ancient debate that I do not wish to
resurrect here, but shouldn't S-Plus developers at least think hard about
modifying or creating another version of a broadly useful apply() -- perhaps
giving up certain error handling or OOP capabilities as the price to pay --
to allow it to be successfully used by the broad majority who need to do
some programming but who do not wish to struggle with the arcana of tricky
subscripting? 

Comments and alternative viewpoints welcome, of course.

Bert Gunter

messages.subject: [S] Summary of "A US Penny is not Fair?"
messages.subject_clean: [S] Summary of "A US Penny is not Fair?"
messages.body_plain:
Hello Everyone and Happy New Year!

I want to thank everyone who responded to my query about any published 
studies on the probability of a head from a flipped penny being 
different from 0.5.  Below my signature I have summarized the 
responses.  The bottom line is that I think my son's savings and loan 
institution fell prey to the belief that if it's on the web, it must be 
true.

The claim on the web site is that "If you toss a penny 10000 times, it 
will not be heads 5000 times, but more like 4950.  The heads picture 
weighs more, so it ends up on the bottom."

I have a hunch that person who wrote this had read about the slight 
difference in weight between the sides of a penny and made up some 
numbers ("more like 4950").  My belief is that the variability in the 
flip of a thumb (for "normal" people, not magicians) more than makes up 
for the slight difference in weight.

Alex McMillan pointed out that "If indeed someone did toss a coin 
10,000 times and came up with 4950 heads, the difference from the 
expected 5,000 is well within sampling variability (P=0.3, Z=1)."

I checked the required sample size to distinguish between p=.495 and 
p=.5.  For alpha=.5, and power=.95, it is about 130,250 for a 2-sided 
test and 108,350 for the one-sided lower alternative.  Anyone have some 
spare time?

Charles Berry thought there might be something in Chance News, but I 
could not find anything in the archive.  Jim Hughes located a pertinent 
article in the American Mathematical Monthly entitled "The Probability 
of Heads" (Vol. 93, p.191, 1986), but I have not had a "chance" to go 
to the library to copy it.

Thanks again to everyone who responded!

Sincerely,

--Steve M.

  _____________
  |    ***    |  Steven P. Millard, Ph.D.
  |     *     |
  | *   *   * |  P robability,      TEL:    206-528-4877
  |   * * *   |  S tatistics &      FAX:    206-528-4802
  |     *     |  I nformation       E-mail: SMillard at ProbStatInfo.com
  |     *     |                     Web:    www.ProbStatInfo.com
  |    ***    |  7723 44th Avenue NE
  |___________|  Seattle, WA 98115-5117 USA

Original Query
--------------
Hello,

This does not relate to S-PLUS, but I thought the readers of this list 
would be interested.

The web page http://www.superkids.com/aweb/pages/humor/10_08.shtml 
contains the following text:

"If you toss a penny 10000 times, it will not be heads 5000 times, but 
more like 4950.  The heads picture weighs more, so it ends up on the 
bottom."

There is no reference listed for this "fact".  Washington Mutual, the 
savings and loan that sponsors the savings program at my son's school, 
recently put out a brochure encouraging kids to save money.  The 
brochure contains some interesting money "facts", including the one 
above.

Does anyone know of research to support the above "fact"?  I know Persi 
Diaconis and others are able to "toss" a coin so that it will always 
land heads, but I'm talking about "random" tossing.  I vaguely remember 
something about seeing a difference in proportion of heads if you spin 
the coin rather than toss it.

Thanks for your time.  I hope everyone is having a great holiday 
season.

***********************************************************************

Alex McMillan:

If indeed someone did toss a coin 10,000 times and came up with 4950 
heads, the difference from the expected 5,000 is well within sampling 
variability (P=0.3, Z=1).  This is one for the books!
---------------------------------------------

Sam Martin:

I remember reading about the spinning thing.  It has to do with the way 
the coin is stamped out.  There is a higher ridge on one side that 
influences the way it will fall.
--------------------------------------------

Bruce McCullough:

I recall reading a discussion of the mythical "fair coin", in which it 
was pointed out that the TRUE probability of heads is not 0.5 but in 
fact varies from coin to coin depending on wear, etc.
I think maybe it was in von Mises, _Prob Stat and Truth_, but I'm not 
sure.
---------------------------------------------

Charles C. Berry:

I think Chance news had an article about a fellow who after retirement 
volunteered to toss a coin many times. I believe Fred Mosteller was 
somehow involved in this. Anyway, you might check the Chance news 
archive and/or the contents of the paper journal.
I don't recall any report of bias on this order...
----------------------------------------------

Andreas Krause:

I can't support you with a reference to the penny toss experiment.
However, I remember that some UK academics ran tests like the one you 
described.  They developped a fair tossing/throwing machine to check 
out "Murphy's Law", that a buttered toast always lands with the 
buttered side down.  As far as I remember, they have also done some 
coin tossing experiments.
If you want to pursue this, you might find a reference on the web.  I 
have no more details, but I think I remember having it seen in the 
"Economist" journal.
-----------------------------------------------

Bob Dawes:

I recall reading a statement similar to the one you
cite in a classic paper on Maximum Entropy
methods (ca. 1968?) by E.T. Jaynes (Physics
Dept., Washington U., St. Louis).  He also
discusses "loaded dice" in some detail.

Okay, Steve, I found it:
Jaynes, Edwin T., "On The Rationale of Maximum-Entropy Methods", Proc. 
IEEE, Vol 70, No. 9, September 1982, pp 939-952.  I scanned it for the 
unfair penny remark and failed to find it.  But I am confident you will 
be interested in Section IV on Loaded Dice, and it provides relevant 
information for evaluating the results of tossing the coin which is, 
after all, a rather easy experiment to replicate.
-----------------------------------------------

Ed Kademan

I can't answer your question but on page 401 of [1] the authors---in
talking about the probability p of getting heads---state that,
"Con artists know that p \approx 0.1 when you spin a newly minted
U.S. penny on a smooth table.  (The weight distribution makes Lincoln's 
head fall downward.)"
If the p is truly as low as .1 I calculate that it should only take 
about 10 or 15 spins to reject the null hypothesis of p = .5.  I just 
tried the experiment with a 1998 penny on a wooden table and out of 20 
spins 10 came up heads.  (Maybe my penny is too worn or my table isn't 
smooth enough.)
[1] Ronald L. Graham, Donald E. Knuth, and Oren Patashnik;
Concrete Mathematics, Second Edition
Addison-Wesley, 1994
------------------------------------------------

Alan Dorfman:

The differential weight between the sides makes a greater difference if 
the coin in spun as opposed to flipped.  In my teaching days, I would 
get intro stat courses to collect data on the spinning; the empirical 
odds were decidedly not 50-50.  A few hundred tosses sufficed to give 
CI's below p = 1/2 (for I think heads).
------------------------------------------------

Jack Lewis:

The following true story might be of interest to you:
Earlier this week,  I was playing with a dreidel, a top that is the 
center
of a game played by Jewish children.  There are 4 sides to the top, 
each
with a different Hebrew letter.  Each person in the game starts with a
certain number of chocolate coins (geld) and you take turns spinning 
the top
until all the chocolate has been eaten (although the rules I learned 
don't
say how fast you are allowed to eat your coins).  The possible outcomes 
are
1. shin - put a coin into the pot
2. nun - do nothing
3. gimmel - take all the coins in the pot
4. hay - take half the coins in the pot

Although the somewhat blunt-nosed dreidel we were using looked 
approximately symmetrical to me and there was just a very small chip on 
one edge, the letter "shin" came up on all but 3 of the first 20 or so 
spins.  The other 3 outcomes were "hay".  Since all of us were 
right-handed, all the spins were clockwise. After awhile I started s  
pinning the dreidel counter-clockwise on my turn.  To my surprise, 
every single time the top was spun counter-clockwise, the letter 
"gimmel" came up!  The letter "gimmel" is opposite "shin" on the 
dreidel.  I had a pretty good chuckle since no one could figure out 
what I was doing differently and it didn't take long before I had all 
the chocolate.  After I told the others my secret, they started 
spinning the dreidel counterclockwise, and they too got "gimmel" every 
time (at least a dozen times total).
Obviously, this was not a scientific experiment (although it would be 
fun to construct such an experiment to get confidence intervals for the 
proportions) but it seems that minor imbalances can lead to major 
differences in outcome proportions with a dreidel.   I'm sure the 
geometry of the object is critical, but if  the hypothesized principal 
carries over to coins, it wouldn't be surprising to see a bias for 
coin-spinning.  So does the direction the coin is spun make a differ  
ence?
--------------------------------------------

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

This will probably affect very few people, but if you are using S-PLUS 
4.5 and programming output with formatting statements that include the 
tab character ("\t"), you will find that tabs are set at 8 characters 
in the Command Window but vary in the Report Window depending on the 
font size.

For example, if you type:

cat("\tOne Tab\n")

this gives 8 spaces before "One Tab" in the Command Window, but gives 
about 7.5 spaces in the Report Window with a 9 point Courier New font 
and about 5.5 spaces with a 14 point Courier New font.

Sincerely,

Date:          Tue, 5 Jan 1999 17:55:45 -0800 (PST)
From:          Chris Thornton <chris at statsci.com>
To:            Falk Huettmann <k9wk at unb.ca>
Subject:       Re: [S] overlay smoothers via GUI  for SPLUS 4.5  Win 95

Dear Mr. Huettmann;

I noticed your question on S-news and since you have current a current
S-plus support subscription I am forwarding an answer.

It is relatively simple to overlay plots using the GUI, tho hardly
intuitive.  I will describe an example where I am plotting ozone and
temperature data from the air dataset, which is included in S-plus.

First I will create a scatter plot using the 2d Graph Toolbar.  I will
select ozone for the x axis and temperature for the y.  I know want to add
a line to this plot.  I click on the 2d plot icon and drag the line 
icon onto the center of 2d scatter plot.  You will notice a grey icon 
representing "line plot" appear in the upper left hand corner of the 
graphsheet. Double click on this icon.  This will open the data to 
plot dialog where you can choose your dataframe, x and y columns.  
Choose air as the dataframe and again ozone as x column and 
temperature as the y column. This will create a line plot that will 
follow the points of the underlying scatter plot.  Put the mouse 
pointer on the line and right click.  Choose Smooth/Sort from the 
menu.  Under the option of "Smoothing Type" you have many options for 
smoothers.  I chose "Smoothing Spline".  You can set any other 
options or arguments that you are allowed too.  Now click on OK. You 
should see your smoother line appear.  You can repeat this as many 
times as you want and select different smoothing types, which will 
overlay on the same graphsheet.  

I hope this helps.  Let me know if you need any further assistance.

Sincerely, 
Chris Thornton

Hopefully we are back to normal.  The problem was caused by a subscriber's
system sending all mail received back to the list as if it were a new
submission.  Unfortunately the software which we use for list
administration, majordomo, does not have an easy way of detecting and
stopping this problem without providing major inconveniences to all
subscribers during normal operations.

messages.subject: Re: [S] Question about "macro" variables
messages.body_plain:
I was going to reply by personal email, but I think there are
some useful general points to make here.

Larry Zaborski asks:
:   
:   I was wondering how one might supply an argument
: to an S+ function so that this argument might
: be used as part of the name of variables and
: objects in S+ code.
: 
: If I were to do what I wanted to do in 
: SAS Macro code, it would look something like this:
: 
:  %macro regit(num);
:    data ds#
:     set full;
:      if a&num ^= .; ** not necessary for SAS proc;
:    proc reg data=ds# model a&num = b c;
:  %mend;
: 
:  %regit(1);
:  %regit(15);

What you should realise is that it is the presence of the `&'
operator in SAS that encourages you to work in this way.  S-PLUS
is not SAS, but it is flexible enough to allow you to do things
this way if you want to.  It doesn't mean it's going to be as
easy or as straightforward as it seems to be in SAS.  If anyone
thinks that makes SAS `better', then I'd say stick to SAS.

The second point I would make is that macros and functions are
NOT the same thing, even roughly.  With the macro above there is
a side-effect in that (in S-PLUS terms) a permanent assignment is
made at the session level.  This is regarded by some (including
me) as in principle dangerous and although it is possible to do
it in S-PLUS, (and some functions like scan() and source() have
to do it), you will have to ask someone else how to do it if you
want to do it yourself.  I don't believe in crippling functions
so that they behave as macros.  So there...  :-)

: With my S+ knowledge, I would do the following to 
: duplicate this:
: 
:  ds1 <- full[!is.na(full$a1),]
:  model1 <- lm(a1 ~ b + c, data = ds1)  # or use 'subset' parameter to
:                                        # combine both of these statements
:  ds15 <- full[!is.na(full$a15),]
:  model15 <- lm(a15 ~ b + c, data = ds15) 
: 
: Is there a way to pass the numbers '1' and '15' to these
: statements so that this could be done with a function call?

Actually there is a simpler way of doing the fitting process:

model1 <- lm(a1 ~ b + c, data = full, na.action = na.omit)
model15 <- lm(a15 ~ b + c, data = full, na.action = na.omit)

I'll show you two ways of writing a function to put the variable
response in the left hand side of the formula, but you will need
to do the assignment up front, in cold blood so to speak

The first method is simpler, but has a minor drawback.  The idea
is to make the formula as a character string, parse it and feed
the result into a call to lm.

fn <- function(n) {
  form <- parse(text = paste("a", n, " ~ b + c", sep = ""))[[1]]
  lm(form, full, na.action = na.omit)
}

The problem is that the call component of the result always has
the formula `formula = form' and so is uninformative and cannot
be flexibly updated.  To make an object with an updatable formula
you have to be a bit more cunning:

fn1 <- function(n) {
  varname <- paste("a", n, sep = "")  # make the name
  eval(substitute(lm(a ~ b+c, full, na.action = na.omit), 
                  list(a = as.name(varname))))  # shove it in & go
}

Now you can say

model1 <- fn1(1)
model15 <- fn1(15)

&c.   If you have many to do, say 1, 2, ..., 15 your best plan is
to put the results in a list:

models <- list()
for(i in 1:15) models[[i]] <- fn1(i)

If, SAS like, you really want 15 separately named objects you can
do it, but it requires the non-standard form of assignment:

for(i in 1:15) assign(paste("model", i, sep=""), fn1(i))

This is also the way I would do it if you were assigning to a
local variable inside the function.

Welcome to S-PLUS.

Bill Venables.

-- 
_________________________________________________________________
Bill Venables, Department of Statistics,    Tel.: +61 8 8303 3026
The University of Adelaide,                 Fax.: +61 8 8303 3696
South AUSTRALIA.     5005.   Email: Bill.Venables at adelaide.edu.au

messages.subject: [S] Programming Question
messages.body_plain:
I'm a first time user of S-plus (I saw it for the first time 2 days
ago) but I have a problem that I need to solve as soon as possible.  Any
help that you could give would be greatly appreciated -- I usually use
Stata, but I'm trying to work on a data set while I'm out of town, and
Stata isn't available here.

     Here's the problem:

     I have two distributions, one a control and one an experimental
group.  The two distributions are overlapping.  I need to determine a
cutpoint at which the probability of being in one group is approximately
equal to the probability of being in the other group.  (This would be easy
were the two distributions approximately normal -- unfortunately, that is
not the case).  

     What I would like to do is write a command that would compute this
cutpoint based on the percentiles of the empirical distribution.  I wanted
to use the bootstrap feature in S-plus, with this command, to come up with
an estimate of this cutpoint.

     Theoretically, I know what I have to do.  But because S-plus is
completely foreign to me, I have really don't know where to start with
this.  Any advice you could give me would be great.  If I haven't done a
good job describing exactly what I'm trying to do, I can explain further.
Thank you.

Dan Neal

messages.subject: Re: [S] Programming Question
messages.body_plain:
Dan Neal writes:

> ... I usually use Stata, but I'm trying to work on a data set while
> I'm out of town, and Stata isn't available here.
> 
>     I have two distributions, one a control and one an experimental
> group.  The two distributions are overlapping.  I need to determine a
> cutpoint at which the probability of being in one group is approximately
> equal to the probability of being in the other group.  (This would be easy
> were the two distributions approximately normal -- unfortunately, that is
> not the case).  
> 
>     What I would like to do is write a command that would compute this
> cutpoint based on the percentiles of the empirical distribution.  I wanted
> to use the bootstrap feature in S-plus, with this command, to come up with
> an estimate of this cutpoint.
> 

I'm not sure what you mean by the "probability of being in one group"
but I assume you mean the conditional probability, given the score
value.  That is, you want to find a critical score x0 such that

        Prob(G1 | x0)  =  Prob(G2 | x0).

Now neither of these probabilities is computable from the distributions,
for normal or any other distributions; they depend on the prior
probabilities of G1 and G2.

What you may be driving at instead is finding a cutpoint x0 where
the two density functions intersect, i.e.,

        Prob(x0 | G1)  =  Prob(x0 | G2).

This is a very tricky problem, nonparametrically, since it involves
empirical density estimation.

For two normal distributions with different means but equal variance,
there is a unique solution, the midpoint of the two means; and that
can be estimated in Splus.  To illustrate the syntax, assume that you
have a continuous variable called X and a dichotomous group variable
called "grp" with values "Ctrl" and "Exper"; then a simple Splus command
would be

   x0.est <- 0.5*(mean(X[grp=="Ctrl"]) + mean(X[grp=="Exper"])).

Of course, the estimation could be done in many other ways; for
example, if you feared some contamination by bad data you could
replace the mean() function by some robust estimator (at worst,
replace "mean" by "median").

These same methods and considerations apply for any two unimodal
symmetrical smooth densities with identical shape and identical
scale but different locations.

Even for two normal distributions with unequal variance, things get
tricky; one method would involve estimating both the means and the
ratio of variances and then solving an appropriate quadratic
(and choosing the root that you really want).  Doing all this
within the bootstrap would be a good learning experience, and
worthwhile, if this is the problem you really need to solve.

If you have enough data to be confident that the distributions are
not normal, your best approach might be to pick a suitable family,
to estimate both densities parametrically, and then set up and
solve a suitable (nonlinear) equation.  There might or might not
be any solutions, and there could easily be several.

A nonparametric approach could be devised, using the Splus
hist() function.  For example, if both distributions lie entirely
between 0 and 20, and histograms with interval length 2 look like
they make sense, you could start by getting the counts for each
group in all 11 intervals:

    c1 <- hist(X[grp=="Ctrl"],  breaks=seq(0,20,2), plot=F)$counts
    c2 <- hist(X[grp=="Exper"], breaks=seq(0,20,2), plot=F)$counts

Next you could change these to proportions (assuming sample sizes
in the two groups are unequal):

    p1 <- c1/sum(c1)
    p2 <- c2/sum(c2)

Then the trick would be to estimate where p1 - p2 = 0, i.e.,
the proportions are equal.  That could be done in a variety of
ways, perhaps depending on how a graph of p1 - p2 (or p1/p2)
plotted versus bin # (1-11) looks.  There isn't any definite
method that I would recommend for arbitrary shapes of distribution.
In any case, such histogram methods could be highly sensitive to
bin locations and widths--the ``breaks'' argument in hist()--
so great care would be needed.

There are all kinds of fancy approaches to nonparametric density
estimation, and perhaps experts will suggest something better
than what I have outlined.  But I doubt that there is any simple
universal approach;  and if this problem is easier using Stata
instead of Splus, I will be truly astonished.

Dave Krantz

but, for samples x1 and x2 of data,

try

from <- min(c(x1,x2))
to <- max(c(x1,x2))
n <- 50
a1 <- density(x1,from=from,to=to,n=n)
a2 <- density(x2,from=from,to=to,n=n)

the first two columns will be the same
compare the third and fourth columns

further interpolation may be had using the approx() function
or by rerunning density() with different from, to and n.

Colin Goodall

help page for na.tree.replace:

WARNING:
       The use of na.tree.replace.all  for  continuous  variables
       with  missing  values  might  be  risky.  These continuous
       predictors  are  replaced  by  factors  based   on   their
       quartiles.  This  migh  be  a good exploratory step but it

which I think also answers your question. It cuts on the quartiles,
sets the NAs to "NA" (as a string) and makes a factor.

If you need to do this, both rpart (at statlib, surrogate splits) and my
Tree function (http://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/pub/S or SWin, case splitting)
have much better strategies for missing values based on imputation.
Treating NA as a separate level is only a good idea when NA is informative
(i.e. didn't do the test because it was bound to be normal) AND you have
lots of examples in the training set.

--

messages.subject: Re: [S] r-square values written into a table
messages.subject_clean: [S] r-square values written into a table
messages.body_plain:
>>>>> "Falk" == Falk Huettmann <k9wk at unb.ca> writes:

    Falk> Hello, I have 15 straight forward linear regressions,
    Falk> and I would like to have the r-square values written
    Falk> into a table, so that I could compare them later,
    Falk> e.g. for a histogram.  I am looking for the command,
    Falk> smartest way, how to write the r-square values in a
    Falk> table/matrix ?

This does not tell us very much.  The `smartest way' will depend
on what features we can assume about the problem.  

For example if the 15 correlations are all possible correlations
between 5 columns of a data matrix, all you need do is

M <- cor(X)
r2 <- M[lower.tri(M)]^2

If they are just a piece of a correlation matrix, for example the
correlations of 3 Y's with 5 X's, then with an obvious notation

r2 <- as.vector(cor(X, Y))^2

On the other hand if the 15 X's and 15 Y's are just any old
irregularly sized vectors, the best thing to do is the obvious
thing: put the X's in one list, the Y's in another in parallel
and use a for() loop:

r2 <- numeric(15)
for(i in 1:15) r2[i] <- cor(X[[i]], Y[[i]])^2

Finally if you don't want to put them in a list but you can
assume that they have regularly formed names, say X1, X2, ...
and Y1, Y2, ...  (as SAS might handle it) then you can use the
get() dodge.  In fact just to show how open-minded and unbigoted
we are, let's make it look a bit SAS-like:

"%&%" <- function(a, b) 
        get(paste(deparse(substitute(a)), b, sep = ""))

r2 <- numeric(15)
for(i in 1:15) r2[i] <- cor(X%&%i, Y%&%i)^2

Now isn't that cute?  :-)

Follow-up question for the S-programming aficionados: Is it
possible, in S3 or in S4, to write a binary operator replacement
function?

Bill Venables

messages.subject: Re: [S] Missing values: Splus and VC++ 5.0
messages.body_plain:
On Sat, 9 Jan 1999, Thomas J. Richards wrote:

> Hello, people experienced with Splus and MS VC++:
> 
> I am trying to interface C and Splus code, Splus 4.5 with NT 4.0, 
> using MS Visual C++ 5.0. Referring to the document
> http://www.mathsoft.com/support/cfortran.pdf, page 15, referenced
> in V&R online complements, I have the following
> sample C program, directly from the text, with my comments:
> 
> #include <S.h>
> //  Yes, %S_HOME%\include IS on my search path in VC++.
> 
> void my_sum(double *x, long *n, double *sum)
> {
>       long i;
>       *sum = 0 ;
>       for (i = 0 ; i < *n ; i++)
>       if (is_na(x[i], DOUBLE)) {
>               //      In above line, "x[i]" should be "x+i", a pointer.
>               na_set(sum, DOUBLE);
>               break;
>       }
>       else
>       *sum += x[i];
> }
> 
> I am trying to make a dll for use with dll.load.  After
> fixing up the pointer error above, I get a .obj file, but I cannot
> get a .dll, due to linker errors, LNK2001, with undefined external 
> _test_na and set_na.  I don't know what to do here.  Thanks in 
> advance for any help.

I don't know what you used, but with the corrected file

cl /MT /Ox /D "WIN32" /I  %SHOME%\include /c test.c
link /dll /out:test.dll /export:my_sum test.obj %SHOME%\lib\Sqpe.lib

works for me. (I am assuming SHOME is set suitably: use %S_HOME% if you
prefer.)  I guess you omitted the import library, which is in the optional
development tools section of the install so you might need to go back to
the install to get it.

For completeness, in S-PLUS 4.5 I used to test this:

dll.load("/temp/test.dll", call="cdecl", symbols="my_sum")

my.sum <- function(x)
 .C("my_sum", as.double(x), n=as.integer(length(x)), s=double(1), NAOK=T)$s

my.sum(1:10)
my.sum(c(1:3, NA))

--

messages.subject: [S] Recent additions to the Hmsic and Design Libraries
messages.subject_clean: [S] Recent additions to the Hmsic and Design Libraries
messages.body_plain:
The Hmisc and Design libraries, for all versions of S-Plus between 3.3 and 4.5,
have been updated.  The new versions will be available tomorrow in
Statlib or late today from the web address below.  Here is a summary of
new capabilities:

Hmisc
--------
The areg.boot function enhances the builtin avas function of Tibshirani to use 
the S formula
language and to bootstrap all results to get confidence intervals.  Soon 
smearing estimates
will be added to this function to allow estimation of untransformed means in 
addition to medians.

transcan now does multiple imputation, and the fit.mult.impute function will do 
the multiple
imputation variance correction for almost any model.

New options have been added to setps to facilitate creating postscript files 
from trellis output.
setpdf has been added to produce nice(r) .pdf files, and an auxiliary function 
topdf() is now
available to convert .ps files to .pdf if you have installed Ghostscript.  The 
setTrellis() function
makes nice defaults for Trellis graphics that will be printed.

cleanup.import has new options for improving imported data frames, especially 
those from Excel.

There is now a plot method for summary(treatment ~ age + sex + 
baseline.cholesterol,
  method='reverse')

The rm.boot function has new options for estimating or using correlation 
patterns in serial data.

There is now a trellis function for empirical cumulative distribution plots, 
ecdf().

There is now a trellis function for dot plots with error bars, Dotplot().  You 
can plot 3- and 5-number
summaries for each data group.  For the latter, two line thicknesses are used 
to show e.g.
two confidence levels.

The new histSpike function draws high-resolution "spike" histograms and also is 
handy for
drawing kernel density estimates.  These can also be added to any of the 4 axes 
of an
existing plot, to show marginal data distributions.  

Pat Burns' (U. Washington) back-to-back histogram function histbackback has 
been added,
with some minor enhancements.

The reShape function will re-shape data.  Matrices (e.g., output of crosstabs() 
or table()) 
can be strung out for display using Trellis,
and strung-out vectors can be reformulated into matrices.  reShape is useful 
for reformatting
serial data with irregular time spacings.

Coming in a week: a help file giving a template for creating, modifying, and 
inspecting data
frames using Hmisc.  Help file will be called data.frame.create.modify.check

Design
----------
A new function rm.boot has been added for dealing with non-randomly missing
longitudinal data using methods of Lavori and Rubin - propensity score matching 
and
multiple imputation.  This function is still very much under development.

Examples have been added to help files for plot.Design and predict.Design 
showing how
to plot predicted curves using Trellis graphics.

An example has been added to the help file for anova.Design to show how to
use the bootstrap to get confidence limits for the ranks of predictors in 
the model, using chi-square - d.f. or other measures  to rank the variables.  
This is to address the problem that arises when a researcher wants to make a 
big deal about a
variable having the largest chi-square in the model.  You may find that a 
variable that is
apparently the most powerful (rank=1) has a 0.95 confidence interval for its 
rank of
[1, 4] out of 7 predictors.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------
Frank E Harrell Jr
Professor of Biostatistics and Statistics
Director, Division of Biostatistics and Epidemiology
Dept of Health Evaluation Sciences
University of Virginia School of Medicine
http://hesweb1.med.virginia.edu/biostat

messages.body_plain:
I am attempting some survival analysis under the exponential model and
am trying to reproduce estimates from the leukemia data, supplied as the
data.frame gehan in the V&R2 MASS library.  Specifically, i am trying to
reproduce the hazard rates under the exponential model for the two
treatments "control" and "6-MP".   The model reproduced from page 355
of V&R2 has estimates of B0 = 3.69  and B1 = -1.53.  Using treatment
contrasts, estimates of the hazard rates for the two groups would be
exp(B0) for the control group and exp(B0 + B1) for the 6-MP group.  
Calculating the hazards by hand (No. of events / total observation time) 
gives an estimate of the hazard rate for the control group of 0.115 which
is clearly not equal to exp(intercept) in the model on page 355.   Could
someone please enlighten me?

Thanks for your time

messages.body_plain:
On Tue, 12 Jan 1999, David Ramsey <RamseyD at landcare.cri.nz> wrote:

>  I am attempting some survival analysis under the exponential model and
> am trying to reproduce estimates from the leukemia data, supplied as the
> data.frame gehan in the V&R2 MASS library.  Specifically, i am trying to
> reproduce the hazard rates under the exponential model for the two
> treatments "control" and "6-MP".   The model reproduced from page 355
> of V&R2 has estimates of B0 = 3.69  and B1 = -1.53.  Using treatment
> contrasts, estimates of the hazard rates for the two groups would be
> exp(B0) for the control group and exp(B0 + B1) for the 6-MP group.  
> Calculating the hazards by hand (No. of events / total observation time) 
> gives an estimate of the hazard rate for the control group of 0.115 which
> is clearly not equal to exp(intercept) in the model on page 355.   Could
> someone please enlighten me?

Yes. You have the groups and signs reversed. `treat' is a factor, with
levels by default in alphabetical order and

> levels(gehan$treat)
[1] "6-MP"    "control"

The `by hand' log rates are -2.159484 for the control group (log(0.115), to
higher accuracy) and -3.686098 for the treatment group.)  The survreg model
is a model for log lifetime (not log rate) and so has the signs reversed.
(Compare the two models at the top of page 352).

This is yet another example in which I find it much safer to look at model
predictions that coefficients. For example

> cbind(gehan, predict(fm))  
   pair time cens   treat       X2 
 1    1    1    1 control 2.159484
 2    1   10    1    6-MP 3.686098
   ....

would have made this clear(er).

messages.subject: [S] Graphical Analysis of Survival Data
messages.body_plain:
Attached to this email are two ascii files. One contains 
a set of S-Plus programs to implement a procedure
described in  D.R. Cox (1979)  "A note on the graphical analysis
of survival data". Biometrika. 66(1):188-190.  The other is 
a description of how to use the programs.  The programs were
written under S-Plus 4.5 running in Windows 95 and tested only
in that environment. 

The original "note" describes a procedure for calculating log-hazard
estimates with independent and constant error.  These 
estimates can be used to graphically assess the 
relationship of hazard with time.  Additionally, direct
use of these estimates may provide a transparent way to
analyse survival data while maintaining reasonable efficiency.

messages.body_plain:
Please excuse that this is not directly related to Splus use.  

I am trying to obtain "refined bootstrap estimates" of prediction error
in regression models, using the procedure given in:

Efron,B. and R.J. Tibshirani. 1993. An Introduction to the Bootstrap.
Chapman & Hall.

on pages 247-252.  The authors suggest (reasonably) that the "optimism"
in the apparent error, given by:

<prediction error when a bootstrapped model is applied to the original data>

minus

<prediction error when the same model is applied to the bootstrap sample>

will be (usually) positive.  I have six linear regression models for which the
optimism is negative, although small -- less than 1% of the original
model's residual squared error.  I would appreciate any comments from
people who are familiar with this procedure as to why this might be (other
than a mistake in my code -- always a possibility, but checked repeatedly).
The models involve 700-800 observations, 3-5 predictors, arcsine/square-root
transformations of the response, and are somewhat to extremely noisy

messages.subject: [S] Is there a simpler way to?
messages.subject_clean: [S] Is there a simpler way to?
messages.body_plain:
Forgive what might be clumsy wording of this question but I'm not exactly
sure how to word it.  

Suppose (for illustration only) I use the function lda from the VR2 library
with a non default na.action (na.action=na.omit).  The object produced by
lda (or many other non-VR2 functions) excludes data which is omitted by the
na.action argument.  If I then follow the lda with the predict function, I
get a matrix that has only the cases actually used by lda in calculating
its results.  If I now use something like table to cross-tabulate the
predicted group against the actual group, I'm faced with a problem.  The
actual group is stored in the original dataset used by lda.  But the
original dataset has some cases that were excluded by the na.action
argument.  The table function doesn't (as far as I can tell) have an
na.action parameter, which means that I cannot use the original dataset in
the table command without running up against the unequal vector length
problem.  Short of creating a second dataset that excludes the missing
data, is there a simpler way of coercing something like table to accept the
first dataset as an argument.

I know this isn't clear, but I've run into this problem a number of
different times but I'm convinced that all I'm doing is propagating a bunch
of extra data.frames or matrices that I then I have remember to destroy
before exiting the program.  I like to reuse and recycle rather than create
unnecessary datasets.

Thanks for your patience in wading through what might be an incoherent post.

messages.subject_clean: [S] Is there a simpler way to?
messages.body_plain:
On Wed, 13 Jan 1999, Marc Feldesman wrote:

> 
> Forgive what might be clumsy wording of this question but I'm not exactly
> sure how to word it.  
> 
> Suppose (for illustration only) I use the function lda from the VR2 library
> with a non default na.action (na.action=na.omit).  The object produced by
> lda (or many other non-VR2 functions) excludes data which is omitted by the
> na.action argument.  If I then follow the lda with the predict function, I
> get a matrix that has only the cases actually used by lda in calculating
> its results.  If I now use something like table to cross-tabulate the
> predicted group against the actual group, I'm faced with a problem.  The
> actual group is stored in the original dataset used by lda.  But the
> original dataset has some cases that were excluded by the na.action
> argument.  The table function doesn't (as far as I can tell) have an
> na.action parameter, which means that I cannot use the original dataset in
> the table command without running up against the unequal vector length
> problem. 

If your fitting process uses all the columns of dataset you can just use

table(na.omit(dataset)["column"], predictions)

>  Short of creating a second dataset that excludes the missing
> data, is there a simpler way of coercing something like table to accept the
> first dataset as an argument.

A better way is illustrated by

crabs[sample(1:200, 20), "FL"] <- NA
cr.lda <- lda(sex ~ FL + RW + CL + CW, data=crabs, na.action=na.omit)
pr <- predict(cr.lda)
keep <- match(dimnames(pr$post)[[1]], row.names(crabs))
table(crabs$sex[keep], pr$class)

This would be considerably easier if extracting a column from a dataframe
gave the row names as names, but it does not.

Actually, for lda there is a much easier way: predict for the original
dataset:

table(crabs$sex, predict(cr.lda, crabs)$class)

as this will predict NA for the rows with missing data (in columns which
are used), but that will not work for logistic models, for example, as the
software is not implemented that way.

So, my strategy would be

(1) See if the predict method can handle it (it probably should but
most will not).
(2) If not, see if the predictions have names. These will be a subset of
the row names  of dataframe and so you can find which rows by match.
(3) If they do not, see if you can get the fit to give you the model frame,
and match its row names against the original. Most na.action methods will
tell you the rows they dropped in the attributes of the model frame.

For example, to use logistic discrimination in my example

cr.glm <- glm(sex ~ FL + RW + CL + CW, data=crabs, na.action=na.omit,
model=T, family=binomial())
pr <- predict(cr.glm, typ="response")
table(crabs$sex[match(names(pr), row.names(crabs))], pr > 0.5)

or

keep <- match(row.names(cr.glm$model), row.names(crabs))
table(crabs$sex[keep],  pr > 0.5)

or look at

attr(cr.glm$model, "na.action")

messages.body_plain:
You are being afflicted by something that I consider a design flaw in 
S, one that I feel fairly strongly about. There are two sets of answers
then to your query: 1) Can S be fixed and 2) how to work around it.  Brian
R has given a comprehensive reply for the second.  

   I posit that the following should work, using the "lung" data set as an
example of one with missing values.

        options(na.action= 'na.omit')
        fit <- lm( time ~ ph.karno + meal.cal, data=lung)
        plot(lung$wt.loss, predict(fit))

That is, the residuals and predicteds from a fit should be 
concordant (same n) with the original data set.  This is true of the
survival functions, and it is fairly easy to make it true for the
other modeling functions.  I presented a paper on this at the Splus
user conference in the fall, and got a very positive response from the
audience, even a positive response from the Splus respresentatives.
   
        Terry Therneau

Backwards compatibility rears its ugly head here, of course. People like
the look of new ideas until their own code breaks! I suggest that
predict(fit, lung) should work (it currently fails, so there is nothing to
break), and have modified all my predict methods so it does (if not in the
released versions yet: trying to be careful not to break things, ...).

Perhaps residuals, fitted, predict should have a `use.all' flag
to be set to T when it is known that NAs are acceptable.

There are lots of design flaws in the model-fitting software: some of us
are urging that they be re-written, but that does not look seductive on the
flyer for a new version of S-PLUS.  That all these functions use old-style
classes is a considerable impediment to using the new features of S-PLUS 5.
And nothing happened about code I submitted a long while ago to make
prediction much safer (by carrying around levels and contrasts in the fit
object.)

pbchen at gsbphd.uchicago.edu (Bin Chen) wrote:

> Hi all. I've read some of the posts relating to this problem, but I'm
> not sure I have the answer yet: I have a fairly large data.frame
> (20MB, 9753 x 258), that I imported from a SAS dataset (took quite a

> 4.5), but short of upgrading hardware, I splitted the data.frame into
> 258 single vectors of size 77KB in a new directory, and then
> "attach('this directory')" will be very fast, and operating with these
> single vectors is much faster too. But then of course I lose the
> flexibilities of working with the original data.frame.
> 
> What would be a better way to do this?

In my experience your proposed approach is the only reasonable
way to analyze really large datasets in S.  I have resorted to
that approach on numerous occasions, some of which have involved
datasets of multiple gigabytes in size.  I generally rename the
separated vectors so they all have a common prefix to avoid
namespace collisions.  This wouldn't be necessary if the
modelling and trellis functions allowed a search position
as an argument to the data= option.  But, alas, they don't.

And note that any analysis that needs to access all the columns
of the data at once (in a single expresssion) will not benefit
much from splitting things up.

--Todd

messages.subject: [S] model selection in glm - logit link vs identity
messages.subject_clean: [S] model selection in glm - logit link vs identity
messages.body_plain:
This is related to a recent discussion about better ways to model data 
     that are proportions.  It has been suggested that rather than doing 
     logit transformations on proportions and then treating them as 
     dependent variables in a least squares regression, that we use a logit 
     link function in a generalized linear model (glm), as this avoids 
     adhoc approaches to dealing with 0's and 1's (McCullagh and Nelder 
     1989).  I like this aspect.  I have a problem where my dependent 
     variable is proportion of seedlings surviving in a quadrat (fixed 
     area) that I want to relate to 4 independent variables.  Using glm I 
     fit both a linear least square regression, glm(surv~ x1 + x2 + x3 + 
     x4,family="gaussian"), and a linear model with logit link and constant 
     variance, glm(surv~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4,family ="quasi"(link = "logit", 
     variance="constant").  Residual plots suggested both models achieved 
     similar homogeneity of residuals and there seemed to be little 
     justification to model the variance function differently than constant 
     (e.g., mu(1-mu) for logit was no improvement.  I thought I might be 
     able to use AIC to pick between these models, but then wondered what 
     "AIC" computation to use as several alternatives have been offered.  
     Below is a summary of deviances and AIC for the 2 models
     
                        identity link               logit link
     
     
     residual deviance      17.245                      16.536
                  df      125                         125      
     
     dispersion              0.138                       0.132
     parameter
     
     AIC                   -252.601                   -258.059  
     
     "quasi" AIC             18.625                     17.856
     
     Now as these really are both least squares regressions, one a linear 
     model (y=b0 + b1x1+ b2x2 + ..)and the other a nonlinear model (y = 
     exp(b0 + b1x1 + b2x2 + ...)/(1+exp(b0 + b1x1 + b2x2 + ...)) where the 
     loglikelihood is for a normal error distribution, I would think to use 
     an AIC based on -2loglikelihood + 2p, where -2loglikelihood = 
     n*log(RSS/n), RSS = residual sums of squares = residual deviance, and 
     p is number of parameters.  But often in the glm literature related to 
     quasi likelihoods where a dispersion parameter is estimated I see a 
     quantity quasi AIC = deviance/estimate of dispersion parameter + 2p or 
     in Venables and Ripley (1994) quasi AIC = deviance + 2p(estimate of 
     dispersion).  Venables and Ripley suggest the estimate of dispersion 
     parameter should be held constant to compare models, but that would 
     make it a constant that effectively could be removed from the formula. 
     All three of these variants of AIC order the models the same (as does 
     just looking at deviance because number of model parameters is the 
     same) but the scale of relative differences is different for the 
     different variants of AIC.  It is the relative differences of AIC that 
     are supposed to be important when comparing models.  What is the best 
     way to compare glm's with different link functions and estimated 
     dispersions (and possibly different number of parameters) using AIC?  
     Or should this not be done?
     
     An interesting issue occurred with estimating the logit link model in 
     3 different packages, S-Plus 4.5, SAS, SYSTAT 7; different parameter 
     estimates or standard errors.  Results below.  Note that deviances 
     (RSS = 16.5365) and estimates of dispersion (MSE = 0.1323) were the 
     same for all packages.  Anyone have any comment on what S-Plus is 
     doing differently than SAS and SYSTAT?
     
     S-Plus                      SAS Insight                   SYSTAT 7
     glm( family=quasi(link         glm (quasi,link=logit,      Nonlinear
      =logit,variance=const)            (variance=normal,        model     
                                         deviance)            (loss = RSS,
                                                              Gauss-Newton)
     
     b0(se)  -0.098 (6.707)        -0.383 (8.295)           -0.383 (6.767)  
     
     b1(se)   0.002 (0.003)         0.002 (0.003)            0.002 (0.003)  
     
     b2(se)  -0.003 (0.002)        -0.003 (0.002)           -0.003 (0.002)  
        
     b3(se)   0.557 (0.208)         0.567 (0.262)            0.567 (0.211)
     
     b4(se)  -0.033 (0.009)        -0.034 (0.011)           -0.034 (0.009)
     
     SYSTAT nonlinear least squares parameter estimates are similar to 
     those from SAS glm but SYSTAT standard errors are more similar to 
     S-plus glm standard errors.  Great discrepancy between SAS/SYSTAT b0 
     estimate and that of S-Plus is disturbing.
     
     Brian Cade (USGS)
     
     brian_cade at usgs.gov

messages.subject: Re: [S] attaching & working with a large data.frame
messages.subject_clean: [S] attaching & working with a large data.frame
messages.body_plain:
I've worked extensively with quite large data sets in Splus.
Generally I find it is best to split the data into a series
of smallish data frames, each of which serves some important
data-analytic purposes.  These modest-sized data frames sometimes
overlap.  Thus, for a recent project, I started by extracting 8
disjoint data frames (totalling 155 columns); I found it convenient
to attach all 8 of them as part of .First().  As the analysis proceeded,
I found it convenient to construct 5 more data frames, each consisting
of some of the variables from various of the original 8 plus some
new variables defined in the course of the analysis.  Most of my work
on that project used these 13 data frames.  Whenever separation became
inconvenient, e.g., I found myself drawing often on elements of
two different data frames in the same sub-analysis, I would simply
put the needed elements together in a new data frame.  The various
data frames are named in a way that makes it fairly easy to remember
what is what, and since they are all reasonably small, it becomes
easy to look at portions of them, or just at the variable names,
to remind oneself of their contents, and of course the analyses
are not held up by long delays in dealing with large data frames.

I find this approach completely satisfactory for my needs.  Perhaps
this is because I don't do "data mining"--or at least, I try not to!

Dave Krantz (dhk at columbia.edu)

messages.subject: Re: [S] glm: how to get standard errors?
messages.subject_clean: [S] glm: how to get standard errors?
messages.body_plain:
: Dear S-Plus users,
: 
: I have an experiment with two factors A and B and I have fitted a
: GLM on these data using:
: 
: > data1.gl.obj <- glm(y ~ A + B, data = data1, family = binomial)
: 
: where y is a 2-column matrix (# of successes, # of failures).
: 
: I would like to get standard-errors of the estimates of some
: linear combinations of the parameters (for example: intercept +
: A_main_effect) in the logit scale. How can I get it in S-Plus?

Formulate the linear combinations in which you are interested as
predictions for potential new cases.  (If you can't do this then
you might have estimability problems, of course.)

Put the dummy cases in a data frame, say newdat.  Then use

> predict(data1.gl.obj, newdata = newdat, type = "link", se.fit = T)

but we warned that the standard errors got from the official
version of predict.glm use an estimated dispersion parameter for
all cases, even for the binomial and Poisson where it is supposed
to be 1.  This is probably not be what you would expect or want.

The version of predict.glm in the MASS library provides the more
usual estimate of standard errors, using the same dispersion
parameter as used by summary.glm, for example.

: Can I use the inverse of the logit link to transform confidence
: intervals got in the logit scale to the probability scale?

Yes, if you know how to interpret the result.  (One advantage of
doing this, of course, is that your confidence interval for the
probability will always be strictly between 0 and 1.  It is
always disconcerting to clients when this is not the case!)

Bill Venables.

messages.subject: Re: [S] Generalised Tree Models and Prediction Error
messages.subject_clean: [S] Generalised Tree Models and Prediction Error
messages.body_plain:
On Fri, 15 Jan 1999, ROSS MCVINISH wrote:

> 
> Hi s-news,
>   
> I need to construct a tree for some binomial data. So far I have just
> been repeating observations in the data frame so as to correspond to the
> correct number of success and failures, is there a quicker way to do this.

Yes, use a tree procedure that allows case weights. For classification,
the only one I know of is my Tree function
(http://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/pub/S. or /pub/SWin for Windows). You also
need a pruning function that allows weights, but treefix in the V&R
bundle does.

> Also, has anyone tried implementing the generalised tree procedure
> described in 'Statistical Models in S' section 9.4.3

I believe that all of that had been implemented by 1990 in the
machine-learning community, not with great success in applications.

>   On a related note, I have been trying to fit tree based models to
> rather small and noise data .  The results of cv.tree() show a huge amount
> of variability in the optimal size of the tree and in the error estimates.

How are you measuring `optimal'?  Are you using the 1se rule?  The aim is
to estimate the differences in error estimates for different k (rather than
tree size), and those are much less variable (over different cv
partitions).

> To get an estimate of the prediction error, after chosing the tree size, I
> have been using the 0.632 bootstrap estimator.  Is there an alternative to
> get around the variability of cross-validation.

Try averaging over many cross-validatory splits (as advocated in Venables &
Ripley, for example).  What is the advantage of 0.632? Most the studies I
have seen (most of which go back to the 1980s) show it to be less accurate
than more conventional means: it may be less variable but it appears to
achieve this by bias.

Interestingly, when I use rpart (which in principle is almost the same
thing as cv.tree) I get less variable tree sizes and (usually) more
accurate predictions.

References for all of this: BDR (1996) Pattern Recognition and Neural
Networks, chapter 7.

--

> Forgive what might be clumsy wording of this question but I'm not exactly
> sure how to word it.  
> 
> Suppose (for illustration only) I use the function lda from the VR2 library
> with a non default na.action (na.action=na.omit).  The object produced by
> lda (or many other non-VR2 functions) excludes data which is omitted by the
> na.action argument.  If I then follow the lda with the predict function, I
> get a matrix that has only the cases actually used by lda in calculating
> its results.  If I now use something like table to cross-tabulate the
> predicted group against the actual group, I'm faced with a problem.  The
> actual group is stored in the original dataset used by lda.  But the
> original dataset has some cases that were excluded by the na.action
> argument.  The table function doesn't (as far as I can tell) have an
> na.action parameter, which means that I cannot use the original dataset in
> the table command without running up against the unequal vector length
> problem. 

If your fitting process uses all the columns of dataset you can just use

table(na.omit(dataset)["column"], predictions)

>  Short of creating a second dataset that excludes the missing
> data, is there a simpler way of coercing something like table to accept the
> first dataset as an argument.

A better way is illustrated by

crabs[sample(1:200, 20), "FL"] <- NA
cr.lda <- lda(sex ~ FL + RW + CL + CW, data=crabs, na.action=na.omit)
pr <- predict(cr.lda)
keep <- match(dimnames(pr$post)[[1]], row.names(crabs))
table(crabs$sex[keep], pr$class)

This would be considerably easier if extracting a column from a dataframe
gave the row names as names, but it does not.

Actually, for lda there is a much easier way: predict for the original
dataset:

table(crabs$sex, predict(cr.lda, crabs)$class)

as this will predict NA for the rows with missing data (in columns which
are used), but that will not work for logistic models, for example, as the
software is not implemented that way.

So, my strategy would be

(1) See if the predict method can handle it (it probably should but
most will not).
(2) If not, see if the predictions have names. These will be a subset of
the row names  of dataframe and so you can find which rows by match.
(3) If they do not, see if you can get the fit to give you the model frame,
and match its row names against the original. Most na.action methods will
tell you the rows they dropped in the attributes of the model frame.

For example, to use logistic discrimination in my example

cr.glm <- glm(sex ~ FL + RW + CL + CW, data=crabs, na.action=na.omit,
model=T, family=binomial())
pr <- predict(cr.glm, typ="response")
table(crabs$sex[match(names(pr), row.names(crabs))], pr > 0.5)

or

keep <- match(row.names(cr.glm$model), row.names(crabs))
table(crabs$sex[keep],  pr > 0.5)

or look at

attr(cr.glm$model, "na.action")

Subject: [S] re: Is there a simpler way

  You are being afflicted by something that I consider a design flaw in 
S, one that I feel fairly strongly about. There are two sets of answers
then to your query: 1) Can S be fixed and 2) how to work around it.  Brian
R has given a comprehensive reply for the second.  

   I posit that the following should work, using the "lung" data set as an
example of one with missing values.

        options(na.action= 'na.omit')
        fit <- lm( time ~ ph.karno + meal.cal, data=lung)
        plot(lung$wt.loss, predict(fit))

That is, the residuals and predicteds from a fit should be 
concordant (same n) with the original data set.  This is true of the
survival functions, and it is fairly easy to make it true for the
other modeling functions.  I presented a paper on this at the Splus
user conference in the fall, and got a very positive response from the
audience, even a positive response from the Splus respresentatives.

Backwards compatibility rears its ugly head here, of course. People like
the look of new ideas until their own code breaks! I suggest that
predict(fit, lung) should work (it currently fails, so there is nothing to
break), and have modified all my predict methods so it does (if not in the
released versions yet: trying to be careful not to break things, ...).

Perhaps residuals, fitted, predict should have a `use.all' flag
to be set to T when it is known that NAs are acceptable.

There are lots of design flaws in the model-fitting software: some of us
are urging that they be re-written, but that does not look seductive on the
flyer for a new version of S-PLUS.  That all these functions use old-style
classes is a considerable impediment to using the new features of S-PLUS 5.
And nothing happened about code I submitted a long while ago to make
prediction much safer (by carrying around levels and contrasts in the fit
object.)

In my experience your proposed approach is the only reasonable
way to analyze really large datasets in S.  I have resorted to
that approach on numerous occasions, some of which have involved
datasets of multiple gigabytes in size.  I generally rename the
separated vectors so they all have a common prefix to avoid
namespace collisions.  This wouldn't be necessary if the
modelling and trellis functions allowed a search position
as an argument to the data= option.  But, alas, they don't.

And note that any analysis that needs to access all the columns
of the data at once (in a single expresssion) will not benefit
much from splitting things up.

From: Brian_Cade at usgs.gov (Brian Cade)
Subject: [S] model selection in glm - logit link vs identity

     This is related to a recent discussion about better ways to model data 
     that are proportions.  It has been suggested that rather than doing 
     logit transformations on proportions and then treating them as 
     dependent variables in a least squares regression, that we use a logit 
     link function in a generalized linear model (glm), as this avoids 
     adhoc approaches to dealing with 0's and 1's (McCullagh and Nelder 
     1989).  I like this aspect.  I have a problem where my dependent 
     variable is proportion of seedlings surviving in a quadrat (fixed 
     area) that I want to relate to 4 independent variables.  Using glm I 
     fit both a linear least square regression, glm(surv~ x1 + x2 + x3 + 
     x4,family="gaussian"), and a linear model with logit link and constant 
     variance, glm(surv~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4,family ="quasi"(link = "logit", 
     variance="constant").  Residual plots suggested both models achieved 
     similar homogeneity of residuals and there seemed to be little 
     justification to model the variance function differently than constant 
     (e.g., mu(1-mu) for logit was no improvement.  I thought I might be 
     able to use AIC to pick between these models, but then wondered what 
     "AIC" computation to use as several alternatives have been offered.  
     Below is a summary of deviances and AIC for the 2 models
     
                        identity link               logit link
     
     
     residual deviance      17.245                      16.536
                  df      125                         125      
     
     dispersion              0.138                       0.132
     parameter
     
     AIC                   -252.601                   -258.059  
     
     "quasi" AIC             18.625                     17.856
     
     Now as these really are both least squares regressions, one a linear 
     model (y=b0 + b1x1+ b2x2 + ..)and the other a nonlinear model (y = 
     exp(b0 + b1x1 + b2x2 + ...)/(1+exp(b0 + b1x1 + b2x2 + ...)) where the 
     loglikelihood is for a normal error distribution, I would think to use 
     an AIC based on -2loglikelihood + 2p, where -2loglikelihood = 
     n*log(RSS/n), RSS = residual sums of squares = residual deviance, and 
     p is number of parameters.  But often in the glm literature related to 
     quasi likelihoods where a dispersion parameter is estimated I see a 
     quantity quasi AIC = deviance/estimate of dispersion parameter + 2p or 
     in Venables and Ripley (1994) quasi AIC = deviance + 2p(estimate of 
     dispersion).  Venables and Ripley suggest the estimate of dispersion 
     parameter should be held constant to compare models, but that would 
     make it a constant that effectively could be removed from the formula. 
     All three of these variants of AIC order the models the same (as does 
     just looking at deviance because number of model parameters is the 
     same) but the scale of relative differences is different for the 
     different variants of AIC.  It is the relative differences of AIC that 
     are supposed to be important when comparing models.  What is the best 
     way to compare glm's with different link functions and estimated 
     dispersions (and possibly different number of parameters) using AIC?  
     Or should this not be done?
     
     An interesting issue occurred with estimating the logit link model in 
     3 different packages, S-Plus 4.5, SAS, SYSTAT 7; different parameter 
     estimates or standard errors.  Results below.  Note that deviances 
     (RSS = 16.5365) and estimates of dispersion (MSE = 0.1323) were the 
     same for all packages.  Anyone have any comment on what S-Plus is 
     doing differently than SAS and SYSTAT?
     
     S-Plus                      SAS Insight                   SYSTAT 7
     glm( family=quasi(link         glm (quasi,link=logit,      Nonlinear
      =logit,variance=const)            (variance=normal,        model     
                                         deviance)            (loss = RSS,
                                                              Gauss-Newton)
     
     b0(se)  -0.098 (6.707)        -0.383 (8.295)           -0.383 (6.767)  
     
     b1(se)   0.002 (0.003)         0.002 (0.003)            0.002 (0.003)  
     
     b2(se)  -0.003 (0.002)        -0.003 (0.002)           -0.003 (0.002)  
        
     b3(se)   0.557 (0.208)         0.567 (0.262)            0.567 (0.211)
     
     b4(se)  -0.033 (0.009)        -0.034 (0.011)           -0.034 (0.009)
     
     SYSTAT nonlinear least squares parameter estimates are similar to 
     those from SAS glm but SYSTAT standard errors are more similar to 
     S-plus glm standard errors.  Great discrepancy between SAS/SYSTAT b0 
     estimate and that of S-Plus is disturbing.

Date: Thu, 14 Jan 1999 16:50:29 -0500 (EST)
From: Dave Krantz <dhk at paradox.psych.columbia.edu>
Subject: Re: [S] attaching & working with a large data.frame

I've worked extensively with quite large data sets in Splus.
Generally I find it is best to split the data into a series
of smallish data frames, each of which serves some important
data-analytic purposes.  These modest-sized data frames sometimes
overlap.  Thus, for a recent project, I started by extracting 8
disjoint data frames (totalling 155 columns); I found it convenient
to attach all 8 of them as part of .First().  As the analysis proceeded,
I found it convenient to construct 5 more data frames, each consisting
of some of the variables from various of the original 8 plus some
new variables defined in the course of the analysis.  Most of my work
on that project used these 13 data frames.  Whenever separation became
inconvenient, e.g., I found myself drawing often on elements of
two different data frames in the same sub-analysis, I would simply
put the needed elements together in a new data frame.  The various
data frames are named in a way that makes it fairly easy to remember
what is what, and since they are all reasonably small, it becomes
easy to look at portions of them, or just at the variable names,
to remind oneself of their contents, and of course the analyses
are not held up by long delays in dealing with large data frames.

I find this approach completely satisfactory for my needs.  Perhaps
this is because I don't do "data mining"--or at least, I try not to!

Dave Krantz (dhk at columbia.edu)
